questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.1 Explain the fulcrum principle and forward tip-over factors
questions.text: Forklift stability is based on what basic principle?

answers.text: Two weights balanced on opposite sides of a fulcrum point
A forklift becomes more stable whenever the load is raised
The rear wheels always carry the entire load weight
The operator’s body weight is the main stabilizing force

explanations.a: Forklift stability is based on the same balancing principle as a teeter-totter, with the front wheels acting as the fulcrum point. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Tire-condition clue: raising a load can move the center of gravity upward and reduce stability.
explanations.c: Travel-position check: the load and forklift are balanced around the front-wheel fulcrum.
explanations.d: Practical safety note: the forklift counterweight and load relationship are the main balance concern.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.1 Explain the fulcrum principle and forward tip-over factors
questions.text: What serves as the fulcrum point on a forklift?

answers.text: The operator’s seat
The front wheels
The steering wheel
The top of the overhead guard

explanations.a: Tip-over prevention check: the operator’s seat is not the pivot point for load balance.
explanations.b: The workbook explains that the front wheels are the fulcrum point for forklift balance. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Configuration-control review: the steering wheel controls direction, not the fulcrum for stability.
explanations.d: Load-handling clue: the overhead guard is a protective feature, not the fulcrum.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.1 Explain the fulcrum principle and forward tip-over factors
questions.text: During forklift stability training, What can contribute to a forklift tipping forward?

answers.text: Driving as far under a stable load as possible before lifting
Keeping the load low and within capacity
Exceeding rated capacity or carrying a load too far forward
Checking the data plate before lifting

explanations.a: Operating-condition review: proper fork placement helps keep the load close and stable.
explanations.b: Side-tip clue: a low, within-capacity load supports stability.
explanations.c: A load that is too heavy or too far from the forklift can move the combined center of gravity forward and cause forward tipping. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: Stability-principle clue: the data plate helps prevent overload and instability.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.1 Explain the fulcrum principle and forward tip-over factors
questions.text: Why should an operator drive as far under the load as possible before lifting?

answers.text: To make the load center farther away from the forklift
To lift with the tips of the forks only
To avoid checking whether the load is secure
To help keep the load close and reduce forward leverage

explanations.a: Capacity-limit review: a farther load center can reduce capacity and stability.
explanations.b: Dynamic-force clue: tip loading can damage equipment and create instability.
explanations.c: Surface-condition note: operators still need to confirm the load is secure and balanced.
explanations.d: Keeping the load close helps control leverage around the front-wheel fulcrum. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.1 Explain the fulcrum principle and forward tip-over factors
questions.text: Which action increases forward tip-over risk?

answers.text: Traveling down a ramp with the load forward when that orientation creates instability
Keeping the load slightly tilted back while traveling
Avoiding sudden braking
Following site procedures for ramps and inclines

explanations.a: Ramp direction and load position affect the combined center of gravity and forward stability. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Data-plate clue: back tilt can help stabilize the load during travel.
explanations.c: Manufacturer-instruction note: sudden braking can affect stability, so avoiding it reduces risk.
explanations.d: Tip-over prevention check: proper ramp procedures reduce tip-over risk.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.2 Explain center of gravity and the stability triangle
questions.keyword: center of gravity and stability triangle
questions.text: During forklift stability training, What is the stability triangle?

answers.text: An imaginary triangle between the drive wheels and the pivot of the steering axle
A warning decal that replaces capacity information
A triangle marked on every load to show its weight
A shape visible only when the forklift is overloaded

explanations.a: The stability triangle represents the area where the combined center of gravity must remain for stability. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Ramps-and-docks note: the stability triangle is a stability concept, not a replacement for the data plate.
explanations.c: Operating-condition review: loads may have markings, but the stability triangle refers to the forklift support area.
explanations.d: Side-tip clue: the stability triangle is a concept used during normal operation.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.2 Explain center of gravity and the stability triangle
questions.keyword: center of gravity and stability triangle
questions.text: What happens if the combined center of gravity moves outside the stability triangle?

answers.text: The forklift becomes safer to turn quickly
The forklift can tip over
The overhead guard prevents all tip-over injuries
The forklift automatically increases capacity

explanations.a: Center-of-gravity note: turning quickly can further reduce stability.
explanations.b: A forklift tends to tip when the combined center of gravity moves outside the stability triangle. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Capacity-limit review: overhead guards do not prevent all tip-over injuries or replace stability control.
explanations.d: Dynamic-force clue: moving outside the stability triangle does not improve capacity.

questions.objective: 3.2 Explain center of gravity and the stability triangle

Raise the load high while traveling through turns
Carry the load low, stable, and within rated capacity
Turn sharply on uneven surfaces

explanations.c: Low, stable, within-capacity loads help keep the combined center of gravity in a safer position. This is the correct answer.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify how load center affects rated capacity
questions.text: A long carpet roll has a load center much farther from the forklift than a pallet. What is the concern?

answers.text: The added leverage can require a larger capacity forklift even if the roll does not weigh much
Long loads always weigh more than pallets
Load center matters only for square boxes
The forklift becomes more stable because the load is longer

explanations.a: A far load center increases leverage and can reduce capacity enough to require different equipment. This is the correct answer.
explanations.b: Tire-condition clue: length and load center can create risk even when weight is not high.
explanations.c: Travel-position check: load center matters for any load shape.
explanations.d: Practical safety note: a longer load can increase leverage and reduce stability.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify how load center affects rated capacity
questions.text: Which statement best addresses load center and rated capacity? What is load center?

answers.text: The vertical height of the overhead guard
The horizontal distance from the load face to the line of action through the load's center of gravity
The distance from the rear axle to the counterweight
The distance between the operator and the steering wheel

explanations.a: Tip-over prevention check: guard height is not the load center.
explanations.b: Load center is the horizontal distance from the load's edge or fork face to the line through the load's center of gravity. This is the correct answer.
explanations.c: Configuration-control review: counterweight position is part of forklift design, not the load center definition.
explanations.d: Load-handling clue: operator position is not the load center.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center
questions.objective: 3.3 Identify how load center affects rated capacity
questions.text: What is the common rated load center for many forklifts noted in the workbook?

answers.text: The operator's arm length
2 inches
24 inches
240 inches for all loads

explanations.a: Operating-condition review: load center is based on load geometry, not operator reach.
explanations.b: Side-tip clue: this is far smaller than the load center stated in the workbook.
explanations.c: The workbook states that most forklifts are rated at a load center of 24 inches. This is the correct answer.
explanations.d: Stability-principle clue: load centers vary by load and rating; the common rating stated is 24 inches.

questions.name: Stability and Load Center

questions.text: What happens when a load is carried at a greater distance than the rated load center?

The load center becomes irrelevant

explanations.c: Surface-condition note: the data plate remains the reference for rated capacity and load center.
